Question: How does the addition of Cr to the HfMoTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy affect its phase composition, microstructure, and room-temperature mechanical properties, specifically regarding the synergy between strength and ductility?. System: HfMoTaTiZr (30.0 at% Hf, 16.1 at% Mo, 30.4 at% Ta, 8.1 at% Ti, 15.4 at% Zr) and HfMoTaTiZrCr0.5 (28.8 at% Hf, 15.5 at% Mo, 29.1 at% Ta, 7.7 at% Ti, 14.7 at% Zr, 4.2 at% Cr). Processing: Vacuum arc melting in an inert gas atmosphere; ingots re-melted at least 5 times to improve chemical homogeneity; weight loss did not exceed 0.5 wt%. Test conditions: Room temperature; Vickers hardness with 0.3 kg load and 15 s dwelling time; compression tests on cylindrical samples (3 mm diameter, 6 mm height) at a ram speed of 0.008 mm s−1 (strain rate 0.001/s). Question: What are the elastic and plastic deformation behaviors of the NbTaTiV refractory high-entropy alloy at room temperature and elevated temperatures, and how do they compare to conventional BCC alloys?. System: Nb23.8Ta25.5Ti24.9V25.8 (nominally Nb25Ta25Ti25V25) BCC refractory high-entropy alloy. Processing: Arc melting under argon atmosphere from 99.99 wt% purity elements, melted 10 times, drop-cast into 4-mm diameter rods, homogenized at 1200°C for 3 days, followed by water cooling. Test conditions: In situ neutron diffraction and compressive testing at room temperature (RT), 500°C, 700°C, and 900°C with a strain rate of 1 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹; Resonant Ultrasound Spectroscopy (RUS) at RT; First-principles calculations at -273°C and RT. Question: How to determine the elastic constants and derived moduli of a NbTaTiV refractory high-entropy alloy using Resonant Ultrasound Spectroscopy (RUS) across a specific frequency range.. System: NbTaTiV HEA. Test conditions: Cylindrical sample corner-mounted between two transducers; frequency swept through the 100- to 650-kHz range; elastic isotropy assumed.. Findings: Elastic constants C11, C12, and C44 were determined using sample dimensions and observed resonances.; Large responses were detected when the frequency corresponded to an eigenfrequency of the sample.; Bulk modulus (K) and shear modulus (G) were determined using Hill's approximations.. Mechanism: The authors assume elastic isotropy and derive elastic constants from the sample's resonant frequencies and dimensions, then calculate bulk and shear moduli via Hill's approximations.. Quote: "Assuming that the elastic isotropy and the elastic constants, ( C 11 , C 12 , and C 44 ), were determined, using sample dimensions, and observed resonances."

Question: What are the magnetic properties of the as-cast high-entropy alloy FeCoNiTi, specifically regarding the origin of its multiple ferromagnetic transitions and the mechanism behind the high coercive field observed in the fcc phase?. System: FeCoNiTi (equiatomic Fe:Co:Ni:Ti = 1:1:1:1) and a C14-dominant variant Fe27Co27Ni17Ti29. Processing: Arc melting of elemental chips/wires (99.9% purity) in an Ar atmosphere on a water-cooled Cu hearth followed by rapid quenching to produce as-cast polycrystalline samples. Test conditions: DC magnetization measured from 50 to 1150 K under 100 Oe; Isothermal magnetization curves at 50, 100, 200, 300, and 400 K; Electronic structure calculations using CPA with PBE potential. Question: Can a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy be successfully fabricated via selective laser melting (SLM) despite processing challenges, and how do its microstructure, hardness, and corrosion resistance compare to traditional superalloys and arc-melted counterparts?. System: NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (nominal equiatomic composition of Nb, Mo, Ta, W powders with 99.9% purity). Processing: Selective laser melting (SLM) using FORWEDO LM120 equipment with a 500 W fiber laser in an argon atmosphere (<20 ppm oxygen); parameters included hatch distance 0.1 mm, layer thickness 0.1 mm, laser power factor 0.8, scanning velocity 250 mm/s, and a triple-pass remelting strategy (3x energy input) to achieve a linear energy density of 2.83 J/mm. Question: How can a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film with superior mechanical and tribological properties be synthesized using a cost-effective single target, and what are the effects of annealing on its adhesion and wear performance?. System: Equimolar CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates. Processing: DC-magnetron sputtering using a single target prepared by partial spark plasma sintering (SPS) of equimolar elemental powders (Cu, Mo, Ta, W, V) at 1000 °C under 40 MPa pressure; film deposition at 500 °C substrate temperature for 120 min in Ar atmosphere (1.16 × 10⁻³ mPa, 150 W power); post-deposition annealing at 300 °C for adhesion improvement. Test conditions: Nanoindentation at 3 mN load; nanopillar compression (440 nm diameter, 3 mN max force); tribological wear tests at room temperature (RT) and 300 °C with 1 N load and 0.1 m/s sliding speed against E52100 alloy steel counterballs.
